# The Value of Disagreement: Why the Best Meetings Don't End in Consensus

There is a common belief, woven deep into how most organizations operate, that a successful meeting is one where everyone leaves nodding. The room reaches agreement, decisions get made, and people file out satisfied. Disagreement, in this view, is a symptom of dysfunction—something to be smoothed over, managed, or suppressed in the name of moving forward.

But this belief deserves a harder look. Agreement is not the same thing as understanding, and a room full of nodding heads may simply be a room full of people who haven't yet discovered what they actually think, or who are too polite, tired, or intimidated to say it out loud. The most dangerous meetings are often the ones that end with everyone apparently on the same page—because the page may be blank.

A genuinely productive meeting, by contrast, can end without consensus and still be a success. What it needs instead is precision: a clear statement of what people disagree about, a clear idea of what evidence would settle the question, and a clear assignment of who will go get that evidence.
